p148.002: For five months, from May to October of A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles stayed at Zebedee's house in Bethsaida, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. A large tent encampment grew up on the beach near the house, and there were always five hundred to fifteen hundred people staying there: people seeking truth, people wanting to be healed, and people who came out of curiosity. David Zebedee was in charge of this tent city. He kept it orderly and clean, and he turned no one away.
p148.003: About once a week the apostles went fishing, sold their catch to the camp, and put the money into the common treasury. While Andrew was in charge of the apostles' work as a whole, Peter was in charge of the school for training evangelists, the people who would preach the gospel. Of all the times Jesus taught, this was the longest period of staying in one place and preparing step by step.
p148.004: 1. A New School of the Prophets
p148.005: Peter, James, and Andrew chose the students, who came from all over the Roman world and even from as far away as India. This school worked by learning and then doing right away. What they learned in the morning, they taught to people on the beach in the afternoon, and in the evening they talked freely about what they had learned and taught that day.
p148.006: Surprisingly, the apostles did not make everyone memorize the same words. Each apostle passed on the same truth in his own way, according to his own experience, and every week, in the question hour, Jesus brought those different points of view into harmony. They made no creed that fixed the teaching into one form. The more than one hundred evangelists trained here later became the foundation for the seventy teachers of the gospel.
p148.008: Elman, a Syrian physician, together with young women and men who served with him, ran for four months what could be called the first hospital of the kingdom of heaven. To all the methods of treatment known at that time, they added prayer and care that encouraged faith. Jesus himself visited the sick more than three times a week and met each person face to face.
p148.009: The Urantia Book says that among the thousand people healed there, there was not a single supernatural miracle. Many of the healings happened when people filled with hope and faith met Jesus' warm, strong personality that drove away fear, and their minds and spirits were changed. The belief of that time that illness was caused by evil spirits was slow to change, but the helpers learned a great deal from watching how Jesus filled patients with faith and confidence.
p148.011: During this time Jesus was alone more often than at any time since his baptism. Whenever the apostles asked why he was away so often, he always answered that he was “⟦Q 148:3.2⟧about the Father's business⟦/Q⟧”. When he went into the hills, he took along two apostles who were free at the time, so all twelve had a chance to be close to him.
p148.012: The writers of The Urantia Book suppose that during these times Jesus was in touch with the high spirit beings who run the universe and was directing universe affairs. The apostles who went with him saw his face change greatly several times, but they did not hear any voices.
p148.014: One evening Thomas asked why people must be born again spiritually, and what evil is. Jesus told apart three things. Evil is breaking the Father's will without knowing it or without meaning to. Sin is breaking it knowingly and on purpose. Iniquity is breaking it stubbornly to the very end and rejecting God's loving plan.
p148.015: Jesus said that people are born imperfect at first, but that imperfection is not sin. Humans are not beings who fell from a perfect state; they are beings who have just begun the long climb toward the perfection of Paradise. A person is never a child of the evil one unless he himself chooses sin and iniquity; from the very beginning he is a child of God. Jesus told them not to tell others about this until he had gone back to the Father.
p148.017: Nathaniel asked why a loving Father lets his children go through so much suffering. Jesus answered that the natural order of this world had been upset many times by the sins of rebels, and that he had come to begin setting it right.
p148.018: Jesus said clearly that the Father does not make his children suffer on purpose, and he does not send suffering to punish wrongdoing. Much suffering is the result of people refusing a better way, and by working wisely, people can overcome much of the pain on earth. We should not blame God for everything we do not understand. Jesus quoted several passages of Scripture that comfort those who suffer, such as “⟦Q 148:5.5⟧A bruised reed shall he not break⟦/Q⟧”.
p148.019: 6. The Misunderstanding of Suffering—Discourse on Job
p148.020: That same evening John asked why people who seem to have done nothing wrong get so sick. Jesus brought up the story of the Book of Job. Job, who had been rich, lost his children, his wealth, and his health, and his three friends made him suffer even more by telling him he was being punished because he had sinned. Jesus said that wealth and prosperity are not a sign of God's favor, and that the Father loves the poor as much as the rich.
p148.021: When Job found no comfort in his friends, he went straight to God. He struggled between faith and doubt until at last he cried out, “⟦Q 148:6.9⟧My Vindicator lives!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that God speaks not in the storm but in a quiet voice within the human heart, saying, “⟦Q 148:6.10⟧This is the way⟦/Q⟧”.
p148.022: Jesus summed up the reasons people suffer in three ways: the accidents of nature and the imperfections of immature beings, the unavoidable results of sin, and the cost of stubbornly holding on to rebellion. But suffering is not a personal judgment sent by God. This conversation changed John's life a great deal.
p148.023: 7. The Man with the Withered Hand
p148.024: On a Sabbath before the second preaching tour, the Pharisee spies from Jerusalem got a man with a withered hand to ask whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. Jesus asked in return whether they would not pull out a sheep that fell into a pit on the Sabbath, and then said, “⟦Q 148:7.2⟧How much more valuable is a man than a sheep!⟦/Q⟧” When the man stretched out his hand, it was made whole.
p148.025: When the people wanted to rush at the Pharisees, Jesus stopped them, saying he had told them to do good, not to do harm. This was the first miracle Jesus did in answer to a challenge from his enemies. It was not to show off his power but a clear protest, so that the Sabbath would not become a chain that binds people. The man, a stonemason, lived thankfully and righteously.
p148.027: During the last week at Bethsaida, three of the spies were deeply moved by what they had seen and heard. In Jerusalem, Abraham, a young member of the Sanhedrin, was publicly baptized, which caused a great stir. He later gave all his property to the apostolic group, which greatly helped send out the hundred evangelists.
p148.028: At this time a self-styled prophet from Baghdad named Kirmeth disturbed the camp by talking about strange visions. Jesus let him speak freely for several days, and the people soon realized on their own that his teachings did not agree with the gospel. Instead of forcing him to stop, Jesus let the people judge for themselves.
p148.030: The day before they left the camp, Zebedee's house was packed with people who wanted to hear Jesus. Just then a paralyzed man from Capernaum, with the help of his friends, climbed up onto the roof, removed the tiles, and was let down on his couch right in front of Jesus. He said that after he was healed he wanted to serve the kingdom of heaven, and when Jesus saw his faith, he said, “⟦Q 148:9.2⟧Son, fear not; your sins are forgiven.⟦/Q⟧”
p148.031: When the Pharisees murmured to themselves that this was blasphemy, Jesus said he would let them know that the Son of Man had authority to forgive sins, and he told the man to get up, take his bed, and go home. The man walked out in front of everyone. Three of the spies believed in Jesus and were baptized. The friends and the sick man who would not give up but found a way show us that the door opens to those who seek with all their hearts.
p149.002: For almost three months, from October to the end of December of A.D. 28, Jesus and the twelve apostles went on the second preaching tour of Galilee together with the 117 evangelists newly trained at Bethsaida. Before they left, the apostles asked Jesus to give a final charge, but he said he did not need to do what someone else could do well, and he left it to James.
p149.003: The purpose of this tour was for the new evangelists to gain experience by actually doing the work. Each apostle took about twelve evangelists with him, and Jesus took only James and John, visiting two towns a day to encourage them. At Bethsaida, David Zebedee kept forty or fifty messengers, people who carried news, and handled communication among the many workers.
p149.005: By this time Jesus was widely known as a healer, and sick people came to him without end. On this tour Jesus did not do any miracle-like healings on purpose, but more than a hundred people were healed on their own without Jesus even knowing. Jesus only said, “⟦Q 149:1.3⟧I perceive that power has gone forth from me⟦/Q⟧”.
p149.006: The writers of The Urantia Book think these healings came from three things meeting together: the living faith of a person who kept seeking healing for spiritual benefit, the deep compassion and power of the Creator Son, and the Father's will. In contrast, a rich widow from Tyre had no interest in the gospel and followed Jesus around offering more and more money, as if God's power could be bought.
p149.008: The Urantia Book says that if Jesus' teachings had been passed on just as they first were, the whole world would have accepted them more easily. When early followers explained them again to suit certain groups of people, they actually made them harder for others to accept. The Urantia Book regrets that seeing Jesus too much as a sacrifice, or stressing only his person, has hidden his teaching, the message that God is our Father and all people are brothers. And it advises that when we meet other religions, we should first recognize the truths we share rather than the differences.
p149.009: The Urantia Book says we should not come to Jesus through miracles, but understand miracles through Jesus. One of the most amazing things about Jesus was the way he treated women. In an age when a man would not even greet his own wife on the street, Jesus made women teachers of the gospel.
p149.010: Jesus was free from superstition and prejudice, and he taught that natural disasters are not God's punishment. He made a clean heart, rather than clean hands, the sign of true religion, but he was not a revolutionary who tore things down; he changed the old only when he could offer something better. The more people knew Jesus, the more they loved him, and The Urantia Book says this is still true today.
p149.012: The people welcomed Jesus, but the religious leaders in Jerusalem grew more and more uneasy and hostile. The Pharisees had built a tightly fixed system of doctrine, but Jesus taught with parables taken from life. The Urantia Book advises that when Jesus used a parable he meant to teach only one main point, so we should not look for hidden meanings in every part of it.
p149.013: When Abraham, the member of the Sanhedrin, and three of the spies became followers of Jesus, the leaders closed their minds even more firmly. Jesus taught that people differ in body, mind, and feelings, but the spirit within them is the same, and only through that spirit can people become one. But the leaders shut out the call of the spirit, and from then on they never stopped plotting to get rid of Jesus.
p149.015: When a young evangelist asked about anger, Jesus said that anger is a sign that the spiritual nature has failed to control the mind and body. Anger harms health, clouds the mind, and gets in the way of the teaching of the spirit within. Jesus quoted the Scripture “⟦Q 149:4.2⟧a soft answer turns away wrath⟦/Q⟧” and urged them to let their hearts be ruled by love.
p149.016: Jesus also stressed a balanced character. Any virtue can become an evil when carried too far: too much sympathy makes the feelings unsteady, enthusiasm turns into fanaticism, courage into recklessness, and too much caution into cowardice. We should be original without being odd, and devout without hypocrisy. What moved people was that Jesus' own life was an example of this balance. Though his enemies set countless traps for him, Jesus was never shaken and never turned to low methods.
p149.018: When Simon Zelotes asked why some people are happier than others, Jesus answered that much depends on being willing to be led by the Father's spirit within. The Scriptures also say, “⟦Q 149:5.2⟧A merry heart does good like a medicine.⟦/Q⟧” Much of human sadness comes from unfulfilled ambition, hurt pride, and fear.
p149.019: Jesus said we should first do our very best, then willingly accept our situation and wisely look for the good in it. When we seek the faith-assurance of being children of God instead of a false peace, true contentment comes. Jesus did not see this world as a “⟦Q 149:5.5⟧vale of tears⟦/Q⟧” but as the “⟦Q 149:5.5⟧vale of soul making⟦/Q⟧”, where eternal souls grow.
p149.021: Philip asked how it could be that the Scriptures tell us to “⟦Q 149:6.1⟧fear the Lord⟦/Q⟧” while Jesus told them not to be afraid. Jesus answered that at first people were taught to honor God out of fear, but over the ages the meaning had grown from terror into awe, and now he had come to lead them from awe to love. God's power brings fear, but when we come to know his goodness and righteousness, we love and worship him with joyful hearts.
p149.022: It is like a little child who at first obeys his parents because he is afraid of them, but as he grows up comes to know what kind of people they are and loves them. Instead of “⟦Q 149:6.7⟧fear God and keep his commandments⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus gave the higher commandment, “⟦Q 149:6.7⟧love God and learn to do his will⟦/Q⟧”. The kingdom of heaven is not a nation ruled by a frightening king; it is a family where the Father and his children are together.
p149.023: Jesus also warned against false humility. Even though a person may be like dust, because the Father's spirit lives within, he is a precious being with a divine destiny. He said we should be deeply humble in heart before God, but humility put on for others to see is childish hypocrisy.
p149.025: On December 30, a rainy day, by evening all the apostles and evangelists had returned to Zebedee's house in Bethsaida. For several days they shared their experiences with one another, and even the older teachers learned a lot from the young evangelists' stories. After that, everyone had two weeks to visit their families and rest.
p149.026: Of the 117, about seventy-five passed the test of real experience and were ready to go on serving. In the process of actually doing what they had learned, the true workers were made known. We too, when we do not stop at knowing things in our heads but try them out in our lives, find that our faith truly grows.
p150.002: In January of A.D. 29, Abner and John's apostles, who had been working at Hebron, came to Bethsaida and held a meeting with Jesus' apostles. John's apostles proposed making it a rule for both groups to pray for the sick while anointing them with oil, but Jesus' apostles refused to be bound by such a rule, and once again Jesus did not take part in the discussion.
p150.003: After that, the apostles, John's apostles, and about seventy-five evangelists who had passed the test gathered and set out on the third preaching tour of Galilee, which lasted seven weeks. The evangelists went out in groups of five to Magdala, Tiberias, Nazareth, and many other towns of central and southern Galilee.
p150.005: Before the tour began, Jesus made a startling announcement: “⟦Q 150:1.1⟧On the morrow we will set apart ten women for the ministering work of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” These women had served at the last encampment and in the tent hospital. Among them were Susanna, the daughter of a teacher at the Nazareth synagogue; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward; and Martha, the older sister of Peter and Andrew. Later Mary Magdalene and Rebecca were added, making twelve. They chose Susanna as their leader and Joanna as their treasurer, and they paid their own way.
p150.006: This was a time when women were not even allowed on the main floor of the synagogue, so making women teachers of the gospel stirred up the whole country. The Urantia Book says it was a declaration that set all women free. From then on, no one could regard women as spiritually inferior. The apostles had heard the saying that “⟦Q 150:1.3⟧in the kingdom of heaven there is neither rich nor poor, free nor bond, male nor female, all are equally the sons and daughters of God⟦/Q⟧”, but when it actually happened they were still greatly surprised.
p150.008: Once the women's corps was formed, women believers could meet Jesus and the apostles much more easily. At Magdala the women went freely into places where it was hard for the apostles to go, and they brought the good news directly to women who had been pushed aside.
p150.009: Here Mary Magdalene entered the kingdom of heaven. Because of many misfortunes and the cold eyes of society, she had ended up in a hard situation, but Martha and Rachel told her that the door of the kingdom was open to her too. Mary became the most outstanding woman teacher of the gospel. The Urantia Book reports that in Jesus' last days, when almost all the apostles had scattered, these women all stood by him, and not one of them denied or betrayed him.
p150.011: At Tiberias the women led the Sabbath service. Joanna led it, and they read from the Scriptures the stories of women in Israel's history, such as Miriam, Deborah, and Esther.
p150.012: That evening Andrew asked whether it was true that a great person is born when a new star appears, and Jesus spoke at length about superstition. The movements of the stars have nothing to do with human lives; astronomy is a true science, but astrology is superstition. The spirits of the dead do not come back to communicate with their families, and charms and spells cannot heal sickness or prevent disaster. Casting lots does not show God's will, and lucky numbers and dream interpretation have no basis. Jesus taught that the only way to be in touch with the spiritual world is through the influence of the Father's spirit within us, the spirit of the Son, and the Infinite Spirit.
p150.013: 4. Sending the Apostles out Two and Two
p150.014: Jesus said, “⟦Q 150:4.1⟧the harvest is plenteous, but the laborers are few⟦/Q⟧”, and he sent the apostles out two by two all over Galilee. He himself stayed behind to teach the young teachers. Jesus urged them to proclaim the saving truth that people are sons of God.
p150.015: Jesus told them not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot destroy the soul. “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧Know you not that the very hairs of your head are all numbered?⟦/Q⟧” God does not forget even one sparrow, so he cares even more for people, who are worth far more. At the same time, Jesus honestly told them that preaching the gospel would not always bring peace, and that when people rejected it, conflict could arise even within families.
p150.016: 5. What Must I Do to Be Saved?
p150.017: At Shunem, Rachel asked how they should answer when women asked, “⟦Q 150:5.1⟧What shall I do to be saved?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: believe the gospel, accept God's forgiveness, and by faith recognize the spirit of God within. Accepting this is what makes us children of God.
p150.018: Jesus said that salvation cannot be bought with money or earned by effort. Salvation is the gift of God. We are not saved because we live good lives; rather, because we know we are already saved children of God, we gladly live right. Entering the kingdom of heaven is free, but to stay in it we must keep growing in grace. Those who heard this were overjoyed, and the women were even happier to know that they too had a part in the plan to build the kingdom of heaven.
p150.020: During the tour Jesus taught many subjects in the evenings: the love of God, humility and meekness, courage and loyalty, music and worship, pride, forgiveness, gossip and envy, doubt and unbelief, and more. With the older apostles away, the young men and women asked questions and discussed much more freely.
p150.021: Jesus visited the different preaching groups one after another, and David's messengers carried news between the groups, which was a great encouragement to the workers who were scattered about. Everyone agreed to gather again at Nazareth on March 4. It was the first time Jesus had visited his hometown since beginning his public work.
p150.023: On the afternoon he arrived in Nazareth, Jesus walked unrecognized past his childhood home and the carpenter shop, and he spent half an hour on the hill he used to climb so often. As he heard the familiar trumpet sound that announced sunset, deep feelings stirred in his heart.
p150.024: But the mood in Nazareth was cold. The people resented that although Jesus had become famous, he had done nothing great in his hometown, and the younger generation was jealous of his fame. On top of that, Jesus' enemies had secretly hired rough men to start a disturbance in the synagogue.
p150.026: On the Sabbath morning the whole town gathered at the synagogue. The service went just as it had when Jesus was a boy, with the prayer praising God who created light and the Shema, the Jewish confession of faith. The scroll that the ruler of the synagogue handed him was actually one Jesus had given to this synagogue when he was young, but no one remembered.
p150.027: Jesus read the passage from Deuteronomy saying that the word of life is not up in heaven or across the sea but “⟦Q 150:8.8⟧in your heart⟦/Q⟧”, and the passage from Isaiah about bringing good news to the poor and proclaiming freedom to the captives. Then he said, “⟦Q 150:8.10⟧Today are these Scriptures fulfilled⟦/Q⟧”, and spoke on “⟦Q 150:8.10⟧The Sons and Daughters of God⟦/Q⟧”. Many people marveled at his wisdom, but in the question time after the service, the troublemakers crowded in.
p150.029: People mocked him, saying he was only the son of Joseph the carpenter, and pushed him to show them a miracle here too. Jesus said that “⟦Q 150:9.1⟧a prophet is not without honor save in his own country and among his own people⟦/Q⟧”, and he answered that the changes grace brings come in response to the living faith of the one who receives them. Jesus could have calmed the crowd gently, but when Simon Zelotes got excited and made ready to fight, the mood turned into a riot.
p150.030: The people dragged Jesus to a steep hill, meaning to throw him off the cliff. At that moment Jesus quietly turned around, folded his arms, and looked at them, and when he walked forward the crowd parted and let him through. Through this the disciples began to realize that the kingdom of heaven would come only through much suffering and disappointment. They gathered again at Bethsaida not as excited victors but as calm and serious preachers of the gospel. Experiences that do not go the way we want can also make us stronger and more mature.
p151.002: In March of A.D. 29, all the groups returning from Nazareth gathered at Bethsaida. Jesus spent most of the Sabbath alone in the hills, and that night he spoke for more than an hour on “⟦Q 151:0.1⟧The mission of adversity and the spiritual value of disappointment⟦/Q⟧”. Those who heard never forgot this lesson for the rest of their lives.
p151.003: Jesus had not yet fully recovered from the sadness of being rejected at Nazareth, and a shadow of sorrow showed on his usually cheerful face. While they waited for the Passover in Jerusalem, the women's corps went from house to house in Capernaum and the nearby towns, teaching the gospel and caring for the sick.
p151.005: Around this time Jesus began for the first time to teach the crowds in parables. One Sunday morning, when nearly a thousand people had gathered on the shore, Jesus sat in Peter's boat and told the parable of the sower. Some seed fell by the wayside and the birds ate it; some fell on rocky ground and withered because it had no root; some was choked by thorns and bore no fruit; but the seed that fell on good ground bore fruit thirty, sixty, and a hundred times over.
p151.006: When Matthew asked why he spoke in parables to people seeking the truth, Jesus answered that those who sincerely wanted the kingdom of heaven would understand the meaning, while those who wanted to trap him would find nothing to pick at.
p151.008: The apostles had a heated debate about the meaning of the parable. Peter explained a hidden meaning for each part, saying for example that the seed is the word of God and the birds are the evil one. Nathaniel explained it a little differently, saying for example that the birds are bad habits and temptations. The apostles split into two sides, each insisting that its own interpretation was right.
p151.009: Then Thomas spoke up and reminded them that Jesus had once taught them not to attach a spiritual meaning to every small part of a story but to pass on just one central truth. Thomas said that the heart of this parable is that no matter how faithfully the gospel is preached, the results will differ according to circumstances we cannot control. Jesus praised him, saying, “⟦Q 151:2.7⟧Well done, Thomas⟦/Q⟧”, but he also said that Peter and Nathaniel had shown very well the danger of forcing meanings onto a parable.
p151.011: The next evening Jesus explained more about parables. Even when listeners are at very different levels, teaching through stories lets each one take in as much as his mind and spirit can hold. Jesus told them not to cover a lamp with a bowl but to put it on a lampstand, and to pay attention not only to how others hear but also, “⟦Q 151:3.1⟧take heed also to yourselves how you hear⟦/Q⟧”.
p151.012: Jesus named many good points of parables. A parable starts from something familiar and leads to understanding something unknown. It wakes up the imagination and the power to think, and it gently plants new truth in the mind while avoiding prejudice. And whenever we see the same scene later, it brings the teaching back to mind. In an age when people believed that spirits caused every event in nature, parables drawn from nature were also a good answer to the leaders' charge that Jesus did his works by the power of evil spirits.
p151.013: That night Jesus added the story of how a seed grows: without the farmer even knowing how, the blade, the ear, and the full grain ripen one after another. The kingdom of heaven grows quietly in the same way.
p151.015: The next day Jesus told more parables from the boat. An enemy sowed weeds in a wheat field, but the owner let them grow together until the harvest so that the wheat would not be pulled up too. The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows until birds nest in it, and like leaven that makes the whole batch of flour rise.
p151.016: The kingdom of heaven is also like a man who found treasure hidden in a field and sold everything to buy that field, like a merchant who sold all he had for one precious pearl, and like a net that catches every kind of fish. From then on Jesus taught the crowds almost only in parables, and in the evenings he explained them to the apostles in more detail.
p151.018: Worn out by the crowds, Jesus took a boat across the lake to rest. On the way, one of the sudden squalls common on the Sea of Galilee came up. It is a wind that forms after sunset, when cold air from the valleys pours down onto the air over the lake that has been warmed during the day. When the sail tore and the boat began filling with water, Peter shook Jesus awake where he was sleeping in the stern.
p151.019: Jesus said, “⟦Q 151:5.5⟧Where is your faith? Peace, be quiet.⟦/Q⟧” and just then the wind died down and the stars came out. The Urantia Book explains that this was a coincidence. Jesus explained that he had spoken not to the wind but to their minds, which were shaken by fear, but the apostles believed it was a miracle of controlling nature. That is because people in those days thought that spirit beings moved every event in nature.
p151.021: On the hillside at Kheresa across the lake, a man named Amos lived in a burial cave. He suffered from an illness that at times threw his mind into great confusion, and he believed he was possessed by many devils. The Urantia Book explains that his trouble was mainly emotional. Jesus took him by the hand, stood him up, and said, “⟦Q 151:6.5⟧Amos, you are not possessed of a devil⟦/Q⟧”, and Amos soon came back to his right mind.
p151.022: Just then, dogs attacked a herd of pigs that no one was watching and drove them over the cliff into the sea. Because these two things happened together, the story spread that Jesus had sent the devils into the pigs, and Amos and most of the apostles believed it too. The townspeople, afraid of losing their pigs, asked Jesus to leave. When Amos wanted to follow him, Jesus said, “⟦Q 151:6.8⟧Forget not that you are a son of God.⟦/Q⟧” and told him to tell his own people what God had done. When we look at life with faith instead of fear, the storms in our hearts can grow calm too.
p152.002: When Jesus came back from Kheresa, a large crowd was waiting for him on the shore at Capernaum. Among them were watchers from the Sanhedrin looking for an excuse to arrest him. Just then Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, fell at Jesus' feet and begged him to come, because his only little daughter was dying. Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:0.1⟧I will go with you.⟦/Q⟧”
p152.003: As they made their way along the crowded street, Jesus stopped and said, “⟦Q 152:0.2⟧Someone touched me.⟦/Q⟧” A woman named Veronica, who had suffered from bleeding for a long time and had spent everything she owned, believed that if she only touched his garment she would be healed. She had secretly touched it, and she was healed. Jesus called her forward and said, “⟦Q 152:0.3⟧Daughter, your faith has made you whole⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book explains that it was not the touch of her hand on his garment but her living faith that healed her. Jesus called her forward so that no one would wrongly think the superstition about touching his garment, or her fear that made her try to be healed in secret, was right.
p152.005: Before they reached Jairus's house, word came that the daughter had already died. Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Fear not; only believe.⟦/Q⟧” He sent out the noisy mourners and went into the room with only the parents and three apostles. Taking the girl by the hand, he said, “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Daughter, I say to you, awake and arise!⟦/Q⟧” and the girl got up and walked.
p152.006: Jesus explained that after a long fever the girl had fallen into a deep coma, and that he had not raised the dead but only awakened her. But the apostles all believed it was a miracle. The Urantia Book says that since someone like Jesus, who was a Creator and also lived in a human body, will not come again, such things cannot be tested by science. Even so, Jesus' spirit is still in people's hearts today, so it tells us not to put limits on what spiritual power might do.
p152.008: To get away from the crowds, Jesus and the apostles went across the lake to a park south of Bethsaida-Julias, but the people followed them, some by hired boats and some on foot. By the third day the crowd had grown to about five thousand men, women, and children, and the food they had brought was gone. At this time a rumor spread quietly among the people that they should make Jesus king right there, and some of the apostles were in favor of it too.
p152.009: When Jesus said he did not want to send the people away hungry, Philip said that even two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough. All that was left were the five barley loaves and two fish that the boy Mark, their errand boy, had with him. Jesus had the people sit down in groups of a hundred, gave thanks, and handed out the bread and fish. Everyone ate their fill, and the leftover pieces filled twelve baskets.
p152.010: The Urantia Book says this was the first and only nature miracle that Jesus did on purpose, having decided on it beforehand. It explains that it was the ordinary natural process that always makes grain and fish grow, only without the time and the visible steps.
p152.012: The well-fed crowd grew excited. The Jews had long expected that when the Messiah came he would send down bread like the manna in the wilderness, so the people all shouted together, “⟦Q 152:3.1⟧Make him king!⟦/Q⟧” At that moment Jesus climbed onto a large rock, raised his hand, and said, “⟦Q 152:3.2⟧you mean well, but you are shortsighted and material-minded⟦/Q⟧”.
p152.013: Jesus said they wanted to make him king not because the truth had enlightened their souls but because their stomachs were full. He said the kingdom of heaven is a spiritual brotherhood, and there is no king who sits on an earthly throne. If they really needed a king, they should place the Father of lights on the throne of each one's heart. Many disappointed people stopped following Jesus from that day. As Jesus went up into the hills alone, he asked Andrew to pray, especially for Peter.
p152.015: Without Jesus, the apostles rowed in low spirits against a strong head wind. Peter, worn out, fell asleep and dreamed that he saw Jesus walking toward them on the water. In the dream Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:4.2⟧Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.⟦/Q⟧” and Peter, walking on the water and starting to sink, cried out, “⟦Q 152:4.2⟧Lord, save me!⟦/Q⟧”
p152.016: While dreaming, Peter actually walked out of the boat and fell into the water, and he woke up only when his brothers pulled him back in. Peter believed for the rest of his life that this had really happened, but The Urantia Book explains that it was Peter's dream and vision.
p152.018: The next day they found that Jesus, with the boy Mark, had walked around the lake in the middle of the night and was back at Bethsaida. Of the five thousand who had eaten the miracle bread, only about five hundred kept following Jesus. Jesus gathered his disciples and scolded them because, after many months of teaching, they were still drawn more by material motives than by spiritual ones.
p152.019: Jesus said that miracles and material wonders cannot lead human souls into the spiritual kingdom. The well-fed crowd was not hungry for the bread of life; they only wanted to make him king so they could keep getting bread without working. The Urantia Book says that this event ended the period of teaching and healing and prepared the way for the last year, when a more spiritual gospel would be preached.
p152.021: While resting at Gennesaret, Jesus talked quietly with the apostles. In Galilee alone there had been more than fifty thousand followers, but in less than a month they had dropped to fewer than five hundred. Jesus wanted the apostles to see for themselves how easily the cheers of people change, so that later they would not rely on such passing excitement.
p152.022: Jesus said that appealing only to the emotions is short-lived and disappointing, and appealing only to the intellect also bears no fruit. Only by appealing to the spirit that lives in a person's mind can character truly be changed and lasting fruit be borne. The apostles slowly began to realize that Jesus would not sit on David's throne and that a hard time of trial was coming soon.
p152.024: In early April, Jesus took only the twelve apostles and quietly went up to Jerusalem for the Passover, avoiding notice. This time he told them not to teach in public, and they stayed mostly at Bethany. When the apostles saw how fierce the hostility toward Jesus had become in Jerusalem, they sensed that a crisis was near.
p152.025: Back at Bethsaida, Jesus asked for permission to speak in the Capernaum synagogue on the Sabbath. He knew it would be his last chance to speak in that synagogue. Even as many people were leaving, Jesus chose truth over popularity. We too can learn the courage to follow the right path rather than the applause of others.
p153.002: When Jesus came back to Bethsaida from Jerusalem, he was silent, as if he were thinking deeply about something serious, and he hardly ate. An uneasy tension spread among the apostles. Nathaniel said they were in the “⟦Q 153:0.2⟧lull before the storm⟦/Q⟧”, and Thomas said it seemed that something out of the ordinary was about to happen.
p153.003: Each apostle had his own ideas. Simon Zelotes hoped that God would step in to help Jesus in some unexpected way, and Judas Iscariot thought Jesus might regret not having become king in front of the five thousand. In the midst of all this, Jesus went out to give a sermon in the Capernaum synagogue that would change an age.
p153.005: On the Sabbath afternoon, sitting in the new synagogue at Capernaum were fifty-three Pharisees and Sadducees from Jerusalem, more than thirty leaders of neighboring synagogues, and even observers sent by Herod. They had come to openly oppose Jesus and his disciples. The leaders asked Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, to stop Jesus from preaching, but he refused, saying, “⟦Q 153:1.7⟧I will not violate my word⟦/Q⟧”.
p153.006: Jesus had now decided not to draw back but to face them boldly. The crisis that began with the feeding of the five thousand came to an end with this sermon, and from then on his popularity drained away like an ebbing tide. The Urantia Book says that in a moment of crisis, people make decisions in the same way they have been choosing between good and evil over and over in everyday life. Jesus let his disciples practice making such choices by going through disappointment. It was also after this sermon that Judas first thought of leaving Jesus.
p153.008: Jesus read the warning from Deuteronomy that a nation will fall if it does not listen to the word of God, and the story of the prophet Jeremiah, who nearly lost his life for warning that the temple would be destroyed. Then he asked how the leaders would treat a teacher who warned of spiritual ruin. Jesus said there was already enough evidence and now they must choose, and, as Joshua had said, “⟦Q 153:2.5⟧choose you this day whom you will serve⟦/Q⟧”.
p153.009: Jesus pointed out that many people had followed him not for the truth but for bread they did not have to work for. And he told them to seek not the food that spoils but the spiritual food that leads to eternal life. Pointing to the pot of manna carved over the synagogue door, he said that the manna their fathers ate was earthly bread, but the Father gives the true bread of life. “⟦Q 153:2.8⟧I am this bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger⟦/Q⟧”.
p153.010: A Pharisee challenged him: “⟦Q 153:2.10⟧are you not Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph, the carpenter?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered that “⟦Q 153:2.11⟧the truth never suffers from honest examination⟦/Q⟧”, and he said that the Father and he are one, and that whoever follows the teaching of the Father's spirit within will in the end come to him. The bread of life Jesus gives is his very life, in which God and man are one.
p153.012: Even after the sermon, the people did not leave but kept firing questions at him for more than three hours. When a Pharisee mocked him, asking whether he meant they should eat his flesh and drink his blood, Jesus explained that he did not mean eating his flesh and blood. He meant that his life, lived according to the Father's will, is the bread of heaven, and that people can become one with him spiritually.
p153.013: When they also complained that his disciples did not keep the ceremony of washing hands before eating, Jesus pointed out that for the sake of human tradition they broke God's commandment to honor their parents. And he said, “⟦Q 153:3.5⟧It is not that which enters into the mouth that spiritually defiles the man, but rather that which proceeds out of the mouth and from the heart.⟦/Q⟧” Evils inside the heart such as jealousy, pride, anger, and lying are what defile a person. The Urantia Book reports that even Peter was not freed from the fear of the traditions about clean and unclean until many years later.
p153.015: Then a Pharisee brought in a young man who was deeply tormented and asked whether Jesus could cast out the devil. Jesus took him by the hand and commanded the evil spirit to come out, and the young man soon came to his right mind. The Urantia Book explains that this was the first case of Jesus actually casting out an evil spirit, and that after the spirit was poured out on all people at Pentecost, such things could no longer happen.
p153.016: When the Pharisees accused him of doing this by the power of the prince of devils, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 153:4.3⟧A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand⟦/Q⟧”. And he solemnly warned that a person who knows something is God's work and yet deliberately insists it is the devil's work is himself refusing forgiveness. Saying that “⟦Q 153:4.4⟧the tree is known by its fruits⟦/Q⟧”, he told them that as they choose now, so they will become. When they demanded a sign, he answered that there would be no other sign besides what they already had.
p153.018: The apostles quietly followed Jesus back to Bethsaida. They were greatly shocked and frightened by the sudden departure of the crowds, the bold attacks of the Pharisees, and the way Jesus had stood up to them so strongly. In the middle of the night Joab, the leader of the evangelists, came back and reported that about a third of the evangelists had left. But although all twelve of the women were shaken, not one of them left.
p153.019: After midnight Jesus came down and said, “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧it is the spirit that quickens; the flesh and all that pertains thereto is of little profit. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said he had known from the beginning that the halfhearted believers would fall away, and he asked the twelve whether they too would desert him. Peter answered, “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧You have taught us the words of eternal life.⟦/Q⟧” and said they would never leave, and everyone nodded. To stay by the truth even when everyone else is leaving: that is the courage of true faith.
p154.002: On the same Saturday night that Jesus preached in the Capernaum synagogue, representatives of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem were in Tiberias pressing Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, to arrest Jesus. But Herod refused. He had received reports that Jesus had refused to be made king by the crowd, and Chuza, an official of his court whose wife was in the women's corps, had told him that Jesus had no interest in politics and only wanted to build a spiritual brotherhood.
p154.003: Herod was also troubled by guilt and superstitious fear over killing John the Baptist, so he did not want to be mixed up in harming Jesus. When the Jewish leaders threatened to accuse him before Caesar, Herod threw them out. As this week went by, Jesus prepared his disciples for the scattering that would soon come.
p154.005: During the first week of May, Jesus held meetings with his trusted disciples at Zebedee's house in the morning, afternoon, and evening. About a hundred people were willing to follow Jesus openly without fearing the opposition of the Pharisees. On Friday of that week, the Capernaum synagogue closed its doors to Jesus and his followers, and Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, stepped down and openly took Jesus' side.
p154.006: Fewer than a hundred and fifty people came to the last meeting by the sea. This was the lowest point of public interest in Jesus. But from this time on, new followers more deeply rooted in true faith began to appear, slowly but steadily. The uncertain period of expecting a material kingdom was over, and the spiritual gospel began to be preached more clearly.
p154.008: The Sanhedrin in Jerusalem passed a decree that no synagogue in Palestine should receive Jesus or his followers. Each synagogue had always run its own affairs, so this was an abuse of power never seen before, and five members of the Sanhedrin resigned. Only the synagogue at Hebron refused to obey, claiming its right to self-rule, and a short time later it burned down.
p154.009: Jesus gave the disciples a week of rest and told them to go home and rest, to play or go fishing, and to pray for the kingdom of heaven. During this time Nathaniel and James were sick for three days with a bad stomach upset. Jesus did not heal them supernaturally; he stayed by their side all night and cared for them himself. The Urantia Book says that Jesus never once used a miracle for his family or his close disciples, because our souls grow not through comfort but through struggling with difficulties and problems.
p154.011: In the middle of May, a second conference was held at Tiberias. The Jewish leaders reported that almost every synagogue had closed its doors to Jesus. At first Herod kept refusing, but after pressure from many sides, he finally agreed that if the Roman governor did not object, the Sanhedrin could arrest Jesus and take him to Jerusalem for a religious trial.
p154.012: On the night of May 21, when word came that the Romans did not object, Herod signed the order allowing the arrest. Herod knew very well that Jesus could not get a fair trial before his enemies in Jerusalem.
p154.014: That same night, fifty leading citizens of Capernaum met in the synagogue and argued until after midnight about “⟦Q 154:4.1⟧What shall we do with Jesus?⟦/Q⟧” Apart from a few who believed Jesus was a prophet, they split into four groups of about the same size. Some said he was a harmless religious fanatic, some said he was a dangerous agitator who would start a rebellion, some said he was in league with the devil, and some said he was out of his mind.
p154.015: Jesus' enemies argued that his teachings were impractical and that the world would fall into chaos if everyone lived by them. The Urantia Book says that some people still say this today, but that a far better civilization could be built on Jesus' teachings, and someday it will be. The world, it says, has never yet seriously tried to live out Jesus' teachings.
p154.017: Before dawn on Sunday, May 22, urgent news reached Bethsaida that Herod had allowed the arrest. David Zebedee immediately called all the disciples to an emergency meeting at seven in the morning. Jesus urged the disciples to keep on with the work of the kingdom, seeking God's guidance no matter what happened. He said the twelve apostles and twelve of the evangelists should go with him, and the women should stay at Bethsaida until he sent for them.
p154.018: David said, “⟦Q 154:5.3⟧I am neither a teacher nor a preacher, but it is in my heart to do this⟦/Q⟧”, and he promised that whatever happened, he would never stop his work of carrying messages. Jesus spoke words of farewell to about a hundred believers. Even with danger right in front of him, his face was brighter and more cheerful than usual as he encouraged their faith, hope, and courage.
p154.020: Just then his mother, Mary, and his brothers arrived. The Pharisees had persuaded Mary that Jesus was out of his mind and that she should take him home before he disgraced the family. In the family, only his sister Ruth wholeheartedly believed in Jesus' mission, and she said she would rather see her brother face death than stop preaching.
p154.021: The house was so full that the family could not get in, and when word came that they were waiting outside, Jesus did not stop speaking but said this: tell his mother and brothers not to worry about him but to trust the Father. Then, pointing to his disciples, he said, “⟦Q 154:6.5⟧whosoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, the same is my mother, my brother, and my sister⟦/Q⟧”. When Mary heard this, she collapsed.
p154.022: The Urantia Book says that Jesus did not abandon his family; it was his family who did not understand him and turned away. Jesus wanted to meet with his family privately after he finished speaking, but at the news that men were coming to arrest him, he had to leave in a hurry. As he got into the boat, he asked that his family be thanked for coming and told to find the courage to do God's will. The Urantia Book says that to everyone who feels misunderstood and unappreciated, Jesus is a friend who understands.
p154.024: So on the morning of May 22, Jesus hurried away by boat to the east side of the lake with the twelve apostles and twelve evangelists. A small boat carrying David's messengers followed them and kept them in touch. From this time on, Jesus truly “⟦Q 154:7.2⟧had not where to lay his head⟦/Q⟧” and began a wandering life, moving to Caesarea-Philippi and the coast of Phoenicia.
p154.025: The officials from Jerusalem arrived too late and spent a week searching around Capernaum in vain. Jesus' family suffered in confusion and was relieved only when Ruth heard the news that Jesus was safe. Even when the people closest to him did not understand him, Jesus did not hate them but treated them with love. We too can learn not to close our hearts at such moments.
p155.002: Having crossed the lake to escape arrest, Jesus and his group of twenty-four spent their first night in the familiar park south of Bethsaida-Julias. Before they went to sleep, Jesus gathered the disciples and told them of his plan to go through Batanea and northern Galilee to the coast of Phoenicia.
p155.004: Jesus quoted the psalm that begins, “⟦Q 155:1.1⟧Why do the heathen rage⟦/Q⟧”, and said these words were coming true before their eyes. But he said the rest of the psalm, about God being angry and the Son breaking the nations with a rod of iron, was a misunderstanding of the mission of the Son of Man. Jesus' kingdom is founded on love, proclaimed in mercy, and built by unselfish service. Jesus told them to serve not out of fear but with faith, and to rejoice not with trembling but with confidence.
p155.005: Jesus pointed out that while his enemies poured all their strength into narrow goals, the disciples hesitated too much, regretted the past, and were lost in empty wishing. He told them not to become narrow, giving the examples of people who have science without religion and people who have religion without science. If we live harmonious lives in keeping with the truth, he said, people will come looking for us on their own.
p155.007: The next day Peter went to Chorazin with the twelve evangelists, and Jesus went to Caesarea-Philippi with the other apostles. Chorazin was the place in Galilee where the fewest people had accepted the gospel. The evangelists preached spiritual truth more earnestly than healing, but for two weeks they reaped almost no fruit.
p155.008: This time was a “⟦Q 155:2.2⟧baptism of adversity⟦/Q⟧” for the evangelists. Without the joy of winning people, they began instead to look more seriously at their own souls and spiritual growth. On the day they met again at Caesarea-Philippi, Jesus told the parable of the sower once more and taught them the meaning of what looks like failure on the outside.
p155.010: The two weeks at Caesarea-Philippi were a hard test for the apostles too. Hardly anyone new came to believe, but they learned a great deal from talking with Jesus every day. They learned that when truth is hardened into rigid creeds and used as boundary lines to divide people, it loses its living power. They also learned that it is good to teach people first to love the brother they can see before loving the God they cannot see.
p155.011: Jesus said that if faith leans only on material things, it will be lost as knowledge of nature grows, but a spiritual religion is not shaken even as science advances. True religion is the sincere loyalty a person gives to his highest and truest convictions; it gives life a high purpose and hope and fills a person with courage. Jesus always warned of the danger of symbols and ceremonies taking the place of living religious experience.
p155.013: The group left Caesarea-Philippi and headed for Sidon on the coast of Phoenicia. On the way, while they ate lunch in the shade of a rock, Peter asked why they had to run from their enemies if God was with them. Thomas asked what the difference was between the religion of the Jerusalem leaders and their own religion, since both served the same God. Jesus said it would help everyone more to answer Thomas's question, and he would talk about it after lunch.
p155.015: Jesus explained three kinds of religion. The first is primitive religion, which comes from fear. The second is the religion of civilized intellect, which leans on the authority of tradition; this is the religion of the mind. The third is true religion, the direct experience of God's goodness and beauty; this is the religion of the spirit. The religion of the mind is propped up by the authority of the church, but the religion of the spirit stands on human experience.
p155.016: The religion of authority looks easy and safe, since all it asks is that you agree with it in your head. But in return for that comfort, a person gives up the most wonderful adventure there is: searching for truth himself and finding God directly. The religion of the spirit means effort, struggle, faith, decision, love, loyalty, and progress. Jesus called each of his disciples by name and asked whether he would go back to the easy way or go with him on the new way, even though it was hard.
p155.017: When they all stood up to answer, Jesus stopped them and told them not to be swept along by their feelings but to find their true answer alone before the Father. After they had prayed, the disciples begged to hear more.
p155.019: Jesus went on. The Father did not speak only to the prophets of old; he is still giving out truth today. He hoped that people would move beyond the authority of tradition to the experience of finding God directly within themselves. He told them not merely to quote the prophets of old but to become living prophets themselves. Jesus also urged them never to look down on the forefathers of Israel, who had searched for God long and patiently.
p155.020: The religion of authority divides people by demanding that they all believe exactly the same things, but the religion of the spirit unites people through the experience of the same spirit, even when they think differently. This is because the same divine spirit lives in every person. Also, there are no separate holy jobs and worldly jobs; for a person led by the spirit, every task is sacred. Jesus said that growing in the ability to feel God's presence matters more than knowing the fact of God.
p155.021: He told them not to try to force proof on others that they know God. The proof is twofold: the fruits of the spirit that ripen in everyday life, and a whole life staked on the search for God. Religion is not a shelter to hide in out of fear; it is an eternal adventure of discovering the God who has come looking for us. The teenage years are a good time to move beyond a faith handed down by others and begin to find a living faith of one's own.
p156.002: On June 10, Jesus and his group arrived near Sidon on the Mediterranean coast and stayed at the home of Karuska, a wealthy woman who had once been cared for at the Bethsaida hospital. They spent almost two and a half weeks in Sidon and the surrounding area.
p156.003: The Sabbath they spent there was very quiet. The disciples thought over the teachings about religion that Jesus had given them on the way, but none of them yet fully understood what they meant.
p156.005: Norana, a Syrian woman who lived nearby, came with her daughter of about twelve, who suffered from convulsions. The disciples tried to send her away, saying Jesus needed rest, but Norana said she would not leave until she had seen him. She asked Thomas why he would send away someone who had come to the Master for help.
p156.006: When Simon Zelotes spoke harshly to her, saying that because she was a gentile, the children's bread could not be thrown to the dogs, Norana did not get angry but answered cleverly. She said she was a believing dog, and even dogs may eat the crumbs that fall from the children's table. Jesus, who had heard this conversation through a window, came out and said, “⟦Q 156:1.7⟧O woman, great is your faith⟦/Q⟧”. From that hour her daughter was well.
p156.007: The next day Jesus told the apostles that they had now seen with their own eyes that gentiles too could have saving faith, and that if the children of Abraham would not believe, the Father's kingdom would be taken by the gentiles.
p156.009: As they crossed a bridge on the way into Sidon, Jesus said, “⟦Q 156:2.1⟧This world is only a bridge; you may pass over it, but you should not think to build a dwelling place upon it.⟦/Q⟧” Here Jesus taught the disciples every morning, and in the afternoons and evenings the disciples preached the gospel in Sidon. Many gentiles joyfully accepted the gospel.
p156.010: The Urantia Book says that in many ways these gentiles understood Jesus better than the Jews did. They saw not only that Jesus was like God but also that God was like Jesus, and that God does not favor any person or nation over another. The Urantia Book says that people did not fail to understand Jesus; they were afraid to understand him.
p156.011: Jesus taught about spiritual progress. A person cannot stand still; he either moves forward or slides back. He told them to forget the past and press forward, and not only to stop doing evil but to learn to do good. Jesus greatly enjoyed Norana's sense of humor, and he was sorry that people who took themselves too seriously lacked humor.
p156.013: At the end of June, the group went north along the coast and taught for a week at Porphyreon and Heldua, and there too many people entered the kingdom of heaven. During this time Jesus went to Beirut to meet a believer named Malach.
p156.014: After that the group went back through Sidon and down south to Tyre. By now the apostles and evangelists were used to working among the gentiles, and they were greatly surprised to see how eagerly the gentiles listened to the gospel and how willingly they believed.
p156.016: For two weeks at Tyre, the apostles and evangelists went out two by two and taught in the city and the area around it, and the people of this port city, who spoke many languages, gladly listened and were baptized. Jesus spoke in public only once, about the Father's love for all mankind, and on that occasion even the doors of the temple of Melkarth were opened to him.
p156.017: Many of the people who made the purple dye that made Tyre famous also believed. When the shellfish used to make the dye grew scarce, they moved far away, even to the ends of the world, to find new beds of them, and wherever they went they spread the gospel that God is our Father and all people are brothers.
p156.019: At Tyre, Jesus told the story of the white lily. The lily keeps its roots in the dark mud, yet lifts its pure white flower high into the sunlight. In the same way, even though a person's roots are in an animal nature, by faith he can lift his spiritual nature into the light of heavenly truth. Jesus, who had been a carpenter, also told them not to be like a foolish carpenter who wastes his time shaping worm-eaten wood, but to lay a strong foundation of character.
p156.020: When Nathaniel asked why we pray about being led into temptation when God does not lead us into it, Jesus explained that people often fall into temptation because of their own selfishness and animal urges. Rather than trying to hold down desires by willpower alone, he said, when we come to love something higher and better with all our hearts, the lower things are forgotten on their own. “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧be not overcome by evil but rather overcome evil with good⟦/Q⟧”.
p156.021: Jesus taught many other things as well. He told them not to be discouraged by the fact that they were imperfect human beings, and not to judge their souls by a single mistake. If we love only those who love us, our lives become narrow, and true self-respect grows along with love for our neighbors. The power not to hold a grudge is the strength of character, and defeat is a mirror that shows us our true selves. Difficulties only make the zeal of those who love truth burn hotter.
p156.023: At the end of July, Jesus and the twelve apostles left Tyre and returned to the Sea of Galilee by way of Ptolemais, Jotapata, Ramah, and Zebulun. The evangelists went back by a different road. Near Kheresa and in the park where the five thousand had been fed, Jesus met with about fifty people who were left of the many believers from Capernaum.
p156.024: While Jesus was away, his enemies thought the movement was finished, and their opposition died down. In fact, people resented the move to close the synagogues, and Herod sent word that he would not arrest Jesus outside of Galilee. The sincere believers who had been sifted out and remained through the trials began to gather again. In this way Jesus prepared for the last year, when he would preach the religion of the spirit of God within the heart. Just as he said, this world is not a home to stay in but a bridge to cross over, so we too can keep our eyes on a higher goal and move forward step by step.
p157.002: Before leaving for Caesarea-Philippi with the twelve apostles, Jesus arranged to meet his family on Sunday, August 7, at the Zebedee boatshop in Capernaum. His mother, Mary, and his brothers and sisters planned to come. But a group of Pharisees from Jerusalem came to Mary's house to find out where Jesus was, and they camped there and waited. Because of this the family could not leave the house, and when Jesus heard about it, he did not go to visit them. So, through no one's fault, Jesus and his family once again missed seeing each other.
p157.004: While Jesus was by the lake with Andrew and Peter, a temple-tax collector came up to Peter and asked, “⟦Q 157:1.1⟧Does not your Master pay the temple tax?⟦/Q⟧” Peter sensed that this was a trap and promised to bring the tax soon. But the money was with Judas on the other side of the lake. Jesus said that a promise once made should be kept, and that they should not give others a reason to take offense. Then he told Peter to catch some fish, sell them, and pay the tax for the three of them.
p157.005: A messenger of David's who happened to overhear this called a fisherman friend, who handed Peter several baskets of fish, and the money from them paid the tax. As Peter was leaving, Jesus said half in jest, “⟦Q 157:1.4⟧maybe you will catch the fish with the shekel in its mouth⟦/Q⟧”, and The Urantia Book explains that this later grew into a miracle story in the Gospels. When the sun set, the three of them crossed by boat to the east side of the lake.
p157.007: The next day more than a hundred believers gathered at Magadan Park near Bethsaida-Julias, and Pharisees and Sadducees came too. They demanded that Jesus show them a sign to prove his authority. Jesus asked how it was that they knew so well “⟦Q 157:2.1⟧how to discern the face of the heavens but are so utterly unable to discern the signs of the times⟦/Q⟧”, and he said that “⟦Q 157:2.1⟧to an evil-minded and hypocritical generation no sign shall be given⟦/Q⟧”.
p157.008: That evening, at a meeting with the believers, they decided that when Jesus came back from Caesarea-Philippi, they would all go on a mission together through the whole Decapolis region. Jesus warned them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, that is, religion that is only on the outside. He told them not to let fear or tradition blind them, but to follow the living Spirit of Truth. True religion brings not only peace but growth that moves forward, he said, and he taught that when love for one's neighbor rises up, we should not hold it back but express it through wise service that meets the neighbor's real needs.
p157.010: Jesus and the apostles headed for Caesarea-Philippi, a beautiful city in sight of Mount Hermon. Jesus hoped the apostles would gain new strength to get through the trials ahead. While they were resting for lunch, Jesus for the first time asked a question about himself: “⟦Q 157:3.3⟧Who do men say that I am?⟦/Q⟧” The apostles answered that people thought of him as a prophet, as John the Baptist, or as someone like Elijah or Jeremiah.
p157.011: Then Jesus stood up, pointed to the apostles, and asked, “⟦Q 157:3.5⟧But who say you that I am?⟦/Q⟧” After a moment of silence, Peter sprang to his feet and cried out, “⟦Q 157:3.5⟧You are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God.⟦/Q⟧” and the other eleven apostles all stood up to show they felt the same. Jesus said this had been revealed to them by the Father, and he told them not to tell anyone for the time being. That night the apostles felt that something great had happened, and they hardly slept.
p157.013: For a long time the apostles had expected Jesus to be the Messiah, the deliverer who would save the Jewish people, and they had been confused by being disappointed again and again. The next day Jesus asked the apostles whether they still held to their confession of the day before, and Peter answered again, “⟦Q 157:4.4⟧We believe that you are the Son of the living God.⟦/Q⟧” By this time Peter was naturally becoming the spokesman for the twelve.
p157.014: Jesus said that this belief was not human knowledge but a revelation that the Father's spirit had given deep in their hearts. And he said that on the rock of this spiritual truth he would build the brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven, a living temple of spiritual fellowship. Each person who realizes that he is a son of God becomes a living stone in this temple. On this day Jesus began to trust the faith of the apostles, all except one.
p157.016: What was new in Peter's confession was that it clearly recognized Jesus as the Son of God, a divine being. The Messiah the Jews of that time were waiting for was an anointed man, not the Son of God. Jesus had tried for a while to change people's ideas about the Messiah little by little, but he found it was not easy. So now he decided to declare boldly that he was both the Son of Man and the Son of God, and to build the kingdom of heaven on this truth, in which human nature and divine nature are joined in one.
p157.018: As Jesus' popularity dropped, the apostles' purse ran empty too, but because David Zebedee had prepared ahead of time, the messengers brought the money they needed. The Urantia Book divides Jesus' earth life into four stages: his childhood, when he only dimly knew who he was; his youth, when he gradually came to understand his divine nature and mission; the time after his baptism, when he worked as a teacher and healer; and the last stage, which began at Caesarea-Philippi and went on to the cross. From now on Jesus appeared not simply as a teacher but as the Son of God who shows us the Father.
p157.019: Jesus told the apostles some astonishing things. He said that anyone who would follow him must be ready to make sacrifices, and that he had come not to be served but to serve and to seek out the lost. He said, “⟦Q 157:6.13⟧He who has seen me has seen the Father.⟦/Q⟧” and also that his kingdom was not of this world and that he must soon leave this world. The apostles listened quietly, bewildered, but they did not understand all he meant.
p157.021: That evening Andrew had a deep talk with each of the apostles, but he was so worried about the attitude of Judas Iscariot that late at night he told Jesus about it. Jesus said there was nothing more to be done, that Andrew should keep trusting Judas, and that he should not speak of this to the other apostles. Judas had been piling up disappointment and resentment over the death of John the Baptist, Jesus' rebukes, Jesus' refusal to become king, the empty purse, and other things. His great mistake was that whenever he went off alone to pray, instead of talking with God, he sank into fear, doubt, and the wish to get even.
p157.022: The other apostles faced the same difficulties, but because they loved Jesus, they stayed with him to the end. On the morning of August 12, Jesus told the apostles to get ready to go up the mountain. There he meant to begin his last work as the Son of God. This story shows that when hard times come, the way to keep faith is not to stay in complaint and doubt but to open our hearts to God.
p158.002: At sunset on August 12, Jesus and the apostles reached the foot of Mount Hermon, where they stayed for two days to prepare their hearts. It was near the place where Jesus had once gone up the mountain alone and officially brought to an end the Lucifer rebellion, the uprising of a heavenly leader against God. Jesus wished that all the apostles could see what was about to happen, but they were not yet spiritually ready to meet heavenly beings. So he decided to take only Peter, James, and John, the three who always went with him when he prayed apart.
p158.004: On the morning of August 15, Jesus climbed Mount Hermon with the three apostles. It is meaningful that this special event took place in gentile country, on a gentile mountain. That day Jesus could have laid everything down and gone back to his place as ruler of the universe, but he chose to follow the Father's will to the end and finish his life on earth.
p158.005: During the night the three apostles fell asleep, and when they woke up, they saw Jesus talking with two shining beings, and his face and form were glowing with heavenly light. Peter thought they were Moses and Elijah, but they were really Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek. Startled, Peter blurted out that they should build three tents there. Then a silvery cloud covered them, and they heard a voice say, “⟦Q 158:1.10⟧This is my beloved Son; give heed to him.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus touched the apostles, who had fallen on their faces, and told them not to be afraid.
p158.007: On the way down the mountain, Jesus told them not to tell anyone what they had seen that day until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. The apostles, who had just seen his glory, were deeply troubled by this talk of death. Peter was so frightened by those words that he changed the subject and asked about Elijah, and Jesus answered that Elijah had already come but people had not received him. Only then did the apostles understand that Jesus was speaking of John the Baptist.
p158.008: Jesus asked them to keep silent because he did not want to encourage the apostles' mistaken idea that he was a Messiah who would save the nation by miracles. And these three were chosen not because they were better than the other apostles, but because they were the ones appointed to go with him whenever he prayed alone.
p158.010: The Urantia Book explains what the transfiguration meant in heaven. Gabriel brought word that the Eternal Son accepted Jesus' mission on earth as fully accomplished, and through the Father Melchizedek came the witness that the Infinite Spirit was also satisfied. But God the Father did not say that the mission was finished; he only bore witness, saying, “⟦Q 158:3.4⟧This is my beloved Son; give heed to him.⟦/Q⟧” So Jesus decided, following the Father's will, to live his human life to its natural end. For the apostles, this event was a sign that Jesus had entered the last stage of his earth life.
p158.012: Meanwhile, at the foot of the mountain, the nine apostles ran into trouble. A man named James of Safed brought his only son, about fourteen years old. The boy suffered badly from epilepsy, and according to The Urantia Book he was also possessed by a wandering, rebellious midwayer, an unseen being between humans and angels, who caused trouble. At that moment the nine apostles were arguing about who would have the highest place in the coming kingdom.
p158.013: Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot stepped forward and boasted, “⟦Q 158:4.6⟧We can heal him⟦/Q⟧”. Simon laid his hands on the boy and gave a command, but the boy had an even worse seizure, and the scribes laughed at the apostles. Andrew too prayed and tried again, but failed. The apostles spent the night ashamed and discouraged, but the father did not give up; he waited for Jesus.
p158.015: When Jesus came back, the father knelt down, told him about his son's suffering, and begged him to heal the boy. Jesus said that the works of faith are not done by the commands of doubting minds, and he had them bring the boy. When the boy had another seizure and fell down, the father pleaded again. Jesus said, “⟦Q 158:5.2⟧All things are possible to him who really believes.⟦/Q⟧” and the father answered, “⟦Q 158:5.2⟧Lord, I believe. I pray you help my unbelief.⟦/Q⟧”
p158.016: Jesus took the boy by the hand and told him to get up, and he commanded the spirit to come out and never enter him again. The boy was healed both of his bodily illness and of his spirit's torment, and from then on he was never sick again. The three apostles who had tasted joy on the mountain came right down to face their companions' failure. The apostles' lives often swung back and forth like this between joy and discouragement.
p158.018: That evening in Celsus' garden, Thomas asked Jesus to teach them why they had failed. Jesus pointed out that instead of praying and waiting, they had been arguing about who would sit in the highest place. And he said that the greatest one in the kingdom is the one who humbles himself and serves his brothers. He taught that spiritual greatness is not in showing off power but in understanding love, the kind of love God has. They failed, he said, because their motives were not pure and were not founded on love.
p158.019: Jesus asked whether they would always need to see miracles before they would believe. And he said that the Son of Man had now entered the last stage, and that he would be killed but would rise again. The apostles were so sad and afraid that they could not ask him anything, but after the resurrection they remembered all of these words.
p158.021: The next day, as the apostles were walking back with Jesus by a quiet road, Andrew asked him whether his words about dying were a parable. Jesus said it was not a parable, and he said plainly that the Son of Man must be rejected in Jerusalem, be killed, and rise again. Then Peter grabbed Jesus by the shoulder and cried out that such a thing must never happen. Peter said it out of love for Jesus, but Jesus felt in those words a temptation to give up the Father's will. So he rebuked him sternly, saying, “⟦Q 158:7.4⟧Get you behind me.⟦/Q⟧” and told him to set his mind not on the ways of men but on the will of God.
p158.022: Then Jesus taught that whoever would follow him must take up his own responsibilities every day and follow, and he asked, “⟦Q 158:7.5⟧What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul?⟦/Q⟧” It was a great shock to the apostles, who had been dreaming of places of honor, but none of them wanted to leave Jesus. Jesus was not sending them alone into battle; he was asking them to follow bravely as he led the way.
p158.024: When they arrived at Peter's house in Capernaum, Jesus asked what they had been talking about so much on the way. The apostles could say nothing, because once again they had been talking about who would be the greatest. Jesus called one of Peter's little children, set the child in the middle of them, and said that whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. He also said that whoever receives one such little child receives him, and he urged them never to look down on the little ones. It is good to remember that true greatness lies not in wanting to be lifted up but in wanting to serve from a lowly place.
p159.002: At Magadan Park nearly a hundred evangelists and disciples, including the women's corps, were waiting. Jesus paired one apostle with one evangelist to form twelve groups and sent them out for four weeks to teach in the cities and villages of the Decapolis. Jesus promised to visit the groups often during that time. On this tour, nothing out of the ordinary, such as miracles of healing, happened at all.
p159.004: At Hippos, Jesus taught about forgiveness. When a shepherd loses one of his hundred sheep, he leaves the ninety-nine and searches for that one until he finds it. Jesus said that God does not just wait for sinners to repent; he goes out looking for them even before they think of repenting. He also said that when a brother does wrong, you should first talk with him quietly, just the two of you. If that does not work, go with one or two friends, and if that still does not work, take it to the whole community. One person should not judge another alone, but the community should judge fairly with its shared wisdom.
p159.005: When Peter asked whether he should forgive his brother up to seven times, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 159:1.4⟧Not only seven times but even to seventy times and seven.⟦/Q⟧” Then he told a story. A king took pity on a servant who owed him the enormous debt of ten thousand talents and canceled the whole debt. But that servant threw a fellow servant who owed him only a hundred denarii into prison. When the king heard this, he was very angry. The lesson is that someone who has been greatly forgiven by God should gladly forgive others too.
p159.007: At Gamala, John said he had seen a man teaching in Jesus' name and had forbidden him because he did not travel with them. Jesus told him not to stop the man. The gospel would soon spread to the whole world, and not every believer could be under the direction of the apostles. Jesus said to “⟦Q 159:2.1⟧reckon that he who is not against us is for us⟦/Q⟧”, and that even when “⟦Q 159:2.1⟧a cup of cold water is given to a thirsty soul⟦/Q⟧”, it is recorded in heaven.
p159.008: John was confused, because this seemed different from what Jesus had said before: “⟦Q 159:2.2⟧He who is not with me is against me⟦/Q⟧”. The earlier saying was about a person's relationship with the truth, and this one was about the relationships among groups of believers. The man John had forbidden, named Aden, kept on teaching afterward and gathered many believers.
p159.010: At Edrei, Jesus told those who teach the gospel what principles they should follow. They should always respect a person's personality and never drag people in by force or clever talk. They should not appeal to fear or pity but to the spirit of God within the person. They should not destroy a person's self-respect, and rather than only pointing out faults, they should generously recognize what deserves praise. Frightening people into believing is a low method, he said, and a loving father does not frighten his children.
p159.011: Jesus said that strong feelings are not the same as being led by the spirit of God. Faith, like the sail of a ship, does not add a load to life but adds power, and the only struggle a believer has is the struggle against doubt. He also told them not to picture him as a man of sorrows, because this gospel is good news overflowing with joy. He told them not to sink into self-pity but to live bravely.
p159.012: Above all, he said that believing does not mean you will escape accidents or troubles. Jesus said, “⟦Q 159:3.13⟧I do not promise to deliver you from the waters of adversity, but I do promise to go with you through all of them.⟦/Q⟧”
p159.014: At Abila, Nathaniel quietly asked Jesus about the Scriptures, because Jesus seemed to treat them differently from the rabbis. In The Urantia Book, Jesus explains that the Scriptures were written by people and reflect the thinking and understanding of the people of their time. So some parts do not show God's love well, and he told Nathaniel not to believe such records as the one saying that the God of love commanded the killing of all one's enemies. At the same time, he said clearly that the Scriptures were the finest collection of religious wisdom and spiritual truth in the world in that age.
p159.015: Jesus said that nothing that has passed through human hands can be completely free of error. The authority of truth lies not in the letters of long ago but in the spirit that lives now. Nathaniel's eyes were opened, yet he was also greatly amazed, and he kept this conversation in his heart for a long time.
p159.016: 5. The Positive Nature of Jesus’ Religion
p159.017: At Philadelphia, when James asked how to choose the good passages of Scripture, Jesus gave examples such as “⟦Q 159:5.3⟧The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 159:5.4⟧You should love your neighbor as yourself.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus taught that God is a loving Father who cares for his children, and so all people are brothers to one another. Worshiping God and serving people was the whole of Jesus' religion.
p159.018: Jesus' religion did not stop at ‘do not’; it was a religion of actively doing good. The saying about turning the other cheek does not mean just taking whatever comes; it means working actively to lead the wrongdoer to a better way. Jesus described three ways to respond to evil: paying back evil with evil, simply putting up with it without complaint, and overcoming evil with good. The third way was the one Jesus wanted. The saying that if someone forces you to carry a load one mile, you should go two miles, means the same thing.
p159.019: Instead of difficult words, Jesus taught with simple comparisons such as salt, leaven, and little children. He brought religion down from heaven to earth and placed it close to people's lives.
p159.021: The Decapolis mission was quite successful. Hundreds of people entered the kingdom, and the apostles and evangelists gained the valuable experience of working on their own without Jesus beside them. On September 16 they all gathered again at Magadan Park to talk over their future plans. David's messengers did the important work of bringing news from the whole region and collecting money to help the apostles' families. Jesus and the apostles rested for a week before their final work, and this was their last rest. The teachings of this paper, to forgive, to reach out first, and to overcome evil with good, can be used just as they are in our own friendships today.
